claim: Neurons rely on translation of synaptic mRNAs in order to generate activity-dependent changes in plasticity.
source: Neurons rely on translation of synaptic mRNAs in order to generate activity-dependent changes in plasticity.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: The study identifies CA1 dendritic transcripts with differentially localized mRNA isoforms generated by alternative polyadenylation and alternative splicing.
source: We identify CA1 dendritic transcripts with differentially localized mRNA isoforms generated by alternative polyadenylation and alternative splicing, including many that have altered protein-coding capacity.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the study combining TRAP and PAPERCLIP approaches.

claim: Many differentially localized mRNA isoforms have altered protein-coding capacity.
source: We identify CA1 dendritic transcripts with differentially localized mRNA isoforms generated by alternative polyadenylation and alternative splicing, including many that have altered protein-coding capacity.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental identification of UR-APA events and alternative splicing events that affect the coding sequence.

claim: FMRP targets are overrepresented among dendritic mRNAs.
source: Among dendritic mRNAs, FMRP targets were found to be overrepresented.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis showing significant overlap between FMRP targets and dendrite-enriched mRNAs.

claim: 383 dendritic FMRP targets were identified in CA1 neurons.
source: Cell-type-specific FMRP-CLIP and TRAP in microdissected CA1 neuropil revealed 383 dendritic FMRP targets and suggests that FMRP differentially regulates functionally distinct modules in CA1 dendrites and cell bodies.
evidence: This is a direct result from the compartment-specific FMRP-CLIP experiments.

claim: FMRP differentially regulates functionally distinct modules in CA1 dendrites and cell bodies.
source: Cell-type-specific FMRP-CLIP and TRAP in microdissected CA1 neuropil revealed 383 dendritic FMRP targets and suggests that FMRP differentially regulates functionally distinct modules in CA1 dendrites and cell bodies.
evidence: This is supported by functional clustering analysis and GSEA showing differential enrichment of functional modules in different compartments.

claim: FMRP regulates approximately 15-20% of mRNAs encoding synaptic functions in the dendrite.
source: FMRP regulates ~15–20% of mRNAs encoding synaptic functions and 10% of chromatin modulators, in the dendrite and cell body, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the functional module analysis of FMRP targets.

claim: FMRP regulates approximately 10% of chromatin modulators in the cell body.
source: FMRP regulates ~15–20% of mRNAs encoding synaptic functions and 10% of chromatin modulators, in the dendrite and cell body, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the functional module analysis of FMRP targets.

claim: In the absence of FMRP, dendritic FMRP targets had increased ribosome association.
source: In the absence of FMRP, dendritic FMRP targets had increased ribosome association, consistent with a function for FMRP in synaptic translational repression.
evidence: This is supported by TRAP-seq data comparing FMRP KO and WT mice.

claim: Increased ribosome association of dendritic FMRP targets in FMRP KO mice is consistent with a function for FMRP in synaptic translational repression.
source: In the absence of FMRP, dendritic FMRP targets had increased ribosome association, consistent with a function for FMRP in synaptic translational repression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in the context of known FMRP function.

claim: Downregulation of FMRP targets involved in chromatin regulation in cell bodies suggests a role for FMRP in stabilizing mRNAs containing stalled ribosomes in this compartment.
source: Conversely, downregulation of FMRP targets involved in chromatin regulation in cell bodies suggests a role for FMRP in stabilizing mRNAs containing stalled ribosomes in this compartment.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on observed downregulation of FM1 targets in cell bodies of FMRP KO mice.

claim: Local translation has been demonstrated in neuronal dendrites and axons.
source: Local translation has been demonstrated in neuronal dendrites and axons (reviewed in Glock et al., 2017; Lin and Holt, 2007; Rangaraju et al., 2017) and allows for rapid and precise changes in the local proteome near active synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Local translation allows for rapid and precise changes in the local proteome near active synapses.
source: Local translation has been demonstrated in neuronal dendrites and axons (reviewed in Glock et al., 2017; Lin and Holt, 2007; Rangaraju et al., 2017) and allows for rapid and precise changes in the local proteome near active synapses.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by the cited reviews.

claim: A brief burst of local translation is necessary and sufficient for induction of the late phase of long-term potentiation (L-LTP).
source: In dendrites, a brief burst of local translation has been shown to be necessary and sufficient for induction of the late phase of long-term potentiation (L-LTP, occurring hours to days after potentiation) (Frey et al., 1988; Kang and Schuman, 1996; Kang et al., 1997) and long-term depression (LTD) (Huber et al., 2000), and inhibiting protein synthesis blocks long-term memory formation (Frey et al., 1988; Sutton and Schuman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: L-LTP occurs hours to days after potentiation.
source: In dendrites, a brief burst of local translation has been shown to be necessary and sufficient for induction of the late phase of long-term potentiation (L-LTP, occurring hours to days after potentiation) (Frey et al., 1988; Kang and Schuman, 1996; Kang et al., 1997) and long-term depression (LTD) (Huber et al., 2000), and inhibiting protein synthesis blocks long-term memory formation (Frey et al., 1988; Sutton and Schuman, 2006).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about L-LTP supported by citations.

claim: A brief burst of local translation is necessary and sufficient for induction of long-term depression (LTD).
source: In dendrites, a brief burst of local translation has been shown to be necessary and sufficient for induction of the late phase of long-term potentiation (L-LTP, occurring hours to days after potentiation) (Frey et al., 1988; Kang and Schuman, 1996; Kang et al., 1997) and long-term depression (LTD) (Huber et al., 2000), and inhibiting protein synthesis blocks long-term memory formation (Frey et al., 1988; Sutton and Schuman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huber et al., 2000.

claim: Inhibiting protein synthesis blocks long-term memory formation.
source: In dendrites, a brief burst of local translation has been shown to be necessary and sufficient for induction of the late phase of long-term potentiation (L-LTP, occurring hours to days after potentiation) (Frey et al., 1988; Kang and Schuman, 1996; Kang et al., 1997) and long-term depression (LTD) (Huber et al., 2000), and inhibiting protein synthesis blocks long-term memory formation (Frey et al., 1988; Sutton and Schuman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: mRNAs are thought to be transported in a translationally repressed state into neuronal processes via transport granules containing RNA-binding proteins.
source: mRNAs are thought to be transported in a translationally repressed state into the neuronal processes via transport granules containing RNA-binding proteins such as the Fragile-X mental retardation protein (FMRP), CPEB1, ZBP-1, and STAU1/2 (Hüttelmaier et al., 2005; Krichevsky and Kosik, 2001; Martin and Ephrussi, 2009).
evidence: This is a model supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transport granules contain RNA-binding proteins such as FMRP, CPEB1, ZBP-1, and STAU1/2.
source: mRNAs are thought to be transported in a translationally repressed state into the neuronal processes via transport granules containing RNA-binding proteins such as the Fragile-X mental retardation protein (FMRP), CPEB1, ZBP-1, and STAU1/2 (Hüttelmaier et al., 2005; Krichevsky and Kosik, 2001; Martin and Ephrussi, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying these proteins in transport granules.

claim: Dendritic targeting elements have been defined for a few mRNAs such as Camk2α, Actb, and Map2.
source: Although dendritic targeting elements have been defined for a few mRNAs such as Camk2α, Actb, and Map2 (Andreassi and Riccio, 2009), and a few RNA-binding proteins have been found to regulate individual mRNAs, such as the interaction between ZBP-1 and the β-actin mRNA (reviewed in Biswas et al., 2019), the functional relationship between the global dendritic transcriptome and individual RNA-binding proteins is still largely unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: ZBP-1 interacts with β-actin mRNA.
source: Although dendritic targeting elements have been defined for a few mRNAs such as Camk2α, Actb, and Map2 (Andreassi and Riccio, 2009), and a few RNA-binding proteins have been found to regulate individual mRNAs, such as the interaction between ZBP-1 and the β-actin mRNA (reviewed in Biswas et al., 2019), the functional relationship between the global dendritic transcriptome and individual RNA-binding proteins is still largely unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The functional relationship between the global dendritic transcriptome and individual RNA-binding proteins is still largely unknown.
source: Although dendritic targeting elements have been defined for a few mRNAs such as Camk2α, Actb, and Map2 (Andreassi and Riccio, 2009), and a few RNA-binding proteins have been found to regulate individual mRNAs, such as the interaction between ZBP-1 and the β-actin mRNA (reviewed in Biswas et al., 2019), the functional relationship between the global dendritic transcriptome and individual RNA-binding proteins is still largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Signaling cascades initiated by synaptic activity lead to dissolution of localized mRNA granules and initiation of translation.
source: For at least some localized mRNA granules, signaling cascades initiated by synaptic activity lead to their dissolution and initiation of translation (Dahm and Kiebler, 2005), but the role of RNA regulatory factors in this process is incompletely understood.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dahm and Kiebler, 2005.

claim: The role of RNA regulatory factors in activity-dependent translation is incompletely understood.
source: For at least some localized mRNA granules, signaling cascades initiated by synaptic activity lead to their dissolution and initiation of translation (Dahm and Kiebler, 2005), but the role of RNA regulatory factors in this process is incompletely understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: FMRP is the RNA-binding protein whose activity is lost in Fragile X syndrome.
source: FMRP, the RNA-binding protein whose activity is lost in Fragile X syndrome, represses translation (Bassell and Warren, 2008; Costa-Mattioli et al., 2009; Darnell et al., 2011; Laggerbauer et al., 2001) and is thought to be a key regulator of activity-dependent local translation in neurons (Banerjee et al., 2018; Bear et al., 2004; Huber et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Fragile X syndrome.

claim: FMRP represses translation.
source: FMRP, the RNA-binding protein whose activity is lost in Fragile X syndrome, represses translation (Bassell and Warren, 2008; Costa-Mattioli et al., 2009; Darnell et al., 2011; Laggerbauer et al., 2001) and is thought to be a key regulator of activity-dependent local translation in neurons (Banerjee et al., 2018; Bear et al., 2004; Huber et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: FMRP is thought to be a key regulator of activity-dependent local translation in neurons.
source: FMRP, the RNA-binding protein whose activity is lost in Fragile X syndrome, represses translation (Bassell and Warren, 2008; Costa-Mattioli et al., 2009; Darnell et al., 2011; Laggerbauer et al., 2001) and is thought to be a key regulator of activity-dependent local translation in neurons (Banerjee et al., 2018; Bear et al., 2004; Huber et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a model supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dendritic FMRP levels are increased upon neuronal activity.
source: Dendritic FMRP levels are increased upon neuronal activity, with evidence for local translation of the FMRP transcript itself (Greenough et al., 2001; Weiler et al., 1997) and kinesin-mediated movement of FMRP-containing mRNA transport granules from the neuronal cell body (Dictenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: There is evidence for local translation of the FMRP transcript itself.
source: Dendritic FMRP levels are increased upon neuronal activity, with evidence for local translation of the FMRP transcript itself (Greenough et al., 2001; Weiler et al., 1997) and kinesin-mediated movement of FMRP-containing mRNA transport granules from the neuronal cell body (Dictenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greenough et al., 2001 and Weiler et al., 1997.

claim: Kinesin mediates movement of FMRP-containing mRNA transport granules from the neuronal cell body.
source: Dendritic FMRP levels are increased upon neuronal activity, with evidence for local translation of the FMRP transcript itself (Greenough et al., 2001; Weiler et al., 1997) and kinesin-mediated movement of FMRP-containing mRNA transport granules from the neuronal cell body (Dictenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dictenberg et al., 2008.

claim: FMRP is proposed to be linked to local signal transduction through calcium-induced post-translational modification.
source: At the synapse, FMRP is proposed to be linked to local signal transduction, potentially through calcium-induced post-translational modification of the protein, which alters the FMRP granule and leads to translation of the mRNAs (Lee et al., 2011; Narayanan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by citations.

claim: Calcium-induced post-translational modification of FMRP alters the FMRP granule and leads to translation of mRNAs.
source: At the synapse, FMRP is proposed to be linked to local signal transduction, potentially through calcium-induced post-translational modification of the protein, which alters the FMRP granule and leads to translation of the mRNAs (Lee et al., 2011; Narayanan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: FMRP knockout neurons show excess basal translation.
source: FMRP knockout (KO) neurons show excess basal translation as well as an inability to produce activity-stimulated translation (Ifrim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ifrim et al., 2015.

claim: FMRP knockout neurons show an inability to produce activity-stimulated translation.
source: FMRP knockout (KO) neurons show excess basal translation as well as an inability to produce activity-stimulated translation (Ifrim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ifrim et al., 2015.

claim: Direct FMRP targets have been identified in the whole mouse brain through CLIP studies.
source: Direct FMRP targets have been identified in the whole mouse brain through CLIP studies (Darnell et al., 2011; Korb et al., 2017), indirectly through ribosome-binding studies (translating ribosome affinity purification [TRAP]; Ceolin et al., 2017; Kumari and Gazy, 2019) or through TRAP together with crosslinking immunoprecipitation (CLIP) (Sawicka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CLIP studies.

claim: FMRP targets have been identified indirectly through ribosome-binding studies (TRAP).
source: Direct FMRP targets have been identified in the whole mouse brain through CLIP studies (Darnell et al., 2011; Korb et al., 2017), indirectly through ribosome-binding studies (translating ribosome affinity purification [TRAP]; Ceolin et al., 2017; Kumari and Gazy, 2019) or through TRAP together with crosslinking immunoprecipitation (CLIP) (Sawicka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to TRAP studies.

claim: FMRP targets have been identified through TRAP together with CLIP.
source: Direct FMRP targets have been identified in the whole mouse brain through CLIP studies (Darnell et al., 2011; Korb et al., 2017), indirectly through ribosome-binding studies (translating ribosome affinity purification [TRAP]; Ceolin et al., 2017; Kumari and Gazy, 2019) or through TRAP together with crosslinking immunoprecipitation (CLIP) (Sawicka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawicka et al., 2019.

claim: Some recent studies have explored FMRP targets specifically in the excitatory CA1 neurons of the mouse hippocampus.
source: Some recent studies have explored FMRP targets specifically in the excitatory CA1 neurons of the mouse hippocampus (Ceolin et al., 2017; Sawicka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: FMRP target genes overlap significantly with autism susceptibility genes.
source: FMRP target genes overlap significantly with autism susceptibility genes and include genes involved in both synaptic function and transcriptional control in the nucleus (Darnell, 2020; Darnell et al., 2011; Iossifov et al., 2012; Sawicka et al., 2019), and loss of FMRP increases translation of chromatin modifiers such as BRD4 (Korb et al., 2017) and SETD2 (Shah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations showing overlap with autism genes.

claim: FMRP target genes include genes involved in both synaptic function and transcriptional control in the nucleus.
source: FMRP target genes overlap significantly with autism susceptibility genes and include genes involved in both synaptic function and transcriptional control in the nucleus (Darnell, 2020; Darnell et al., 2011; Iossifov et al., 2012; Sawicka et al., 2019), and loss of FMRP increases translation of chromatin modifiers such as BRD4 (Korb et al., 2017) and SETD2 (Shah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing FMRP targets.

claim: Loss of FMRP increases translation of chromatin modifiers such as BRD4.
source: FMRP target genes overlap significantly with autism susceptibility genes and include genes involved in both synaptic function and transcriptional control in the nucleus (Darnell, 2020; Darnell et al., 2011; Iossifov et al., 2012; Sawicka et al., 2019), and loss of FMRP increases translation of chromatin modifiers such as BRD4 (Korb et al., 2017) and SETD2 (Shah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Korb et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of FMRP increases translation of chromatin modifiers such as SETD2.
source: FMRP target genes overlap significantly with autism susceptibility genes and include genes involved in both synaptic function and transcriptional control in the nucleus (Darnell, 2020; Darnell et al., 2011; Iossifov et al., 2012; Sawicka et al., 2019), and loss of FMRP increases translation of chromatin modifiers such as BRD4 (Korb et al., 2017) and SETD2 (Shah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shah et al., 2020.

claim: A model has been suggested in which FMRP regulates the stoichiometry of its targets globally by translational control of transcription regulators in the cell body and locally by enabling activity-dependent local translation of synaptic proteins in dendrites.
source: These and other observations have suggested a model in which FMRP regulates the stoichiometry of its targets in two ways: globally, by translational control of transcription regulators in the cell body, and locally, by enabling activity-dependent local translation of synaptic proteins in dendrites (Darnell, 2020), but it is still unclear the extent to which such regulation occurs simultaneously in a single neuron.
evidence: This is a model proposed in the literature, supported by citation to Darnell, 2020.

claim: It is still unclear the extent to which FMRP regulation occurs simultaneously in a single neuron.
source: These and other observations have suggested a model in which FMRP regulates the stoichiometry of its targets in two ways: globally, by translational control of transcription regulators in the cell body, and locally, by enabling activity-dependent local translation of synaptic proteins in dendrites (Darnell, 2020), but it is still unclear the extent to which such regulation occurs simultaneously in a single neuron.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: 2058 mRNAs were identified as dendrite-present in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: We identified two groups of dendritic, ribosome-bound mRNAs: dendrite-present (significantly enriched in CA1 neuropil TRAP-seq over CA1 neuropil bulk RNA-seq; 2058 mRNAs) and dendrite-enriched (dendrite-present and also significantly enriched in CA1 neuropil TRAP over cell bodies TRAP; 1211 mRNAs; Figure 1B, see Supplementary file 1A and B for a full list of mRNAs identified).
evidence: This is a direct result from the TRAP-seq experiments.

claim: 1211 mRNAs were identified as dendrite-enriched in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: We identified two groups of dendritic, ribosome-bound mRNAs: dendrite-present (significantly enriched in CA1 neuropil TRAP-seq over CA1 neuropil bulk RNA-seq; 2058 mRNAs) and dendrite-enriched (dendrite-present and also significantly enriched in CA1 neuropil TRAP over cell bodies TRAP; 1211 mRNAs; Figure 1B, see Supplementary file 1A and B for a full list of mRNAs identified).
evidence: This is a direct result from the TRAP-seq experiments.

claim: 689 (34%) of the dendrite-present mRNAs were previously identified in bulk RNA-seq of the microdissected rat CA1 neuropil.
source: 689 (34%) of the dendrite-present mRNAs were previously identified in bulk RNA-seq of the microdissected rat CA1 neuropil (Cajigas et al., 2012), and these RNAs were found to be significantly enriched in dendrites (CA1 neuropil TRAP vs. bulk RNA-seq; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from Cajigas et al., 2012.

claim: Previously identified dendritic mRNAs from rat studies were found to be significantly enriched in dendrites in the current mouse study.
source: 689 (34%) of the dendrite-present mRNAs were previously identified in bulk RNA-seq of the microdissected rat CA1 neuropil (Cajigas et al., 2012), and these RNAs were found to be significantly enriched in dendrites (CA1 neuropil TRAP vs. bulk RNA-seq; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Dendrite-enriched mRNAs are significantly longer than the whole-cell transcriptome identified in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: The identified dendrite-enriched mRNAs were significantly longer than the whole-cell transcriptome identified in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Sawicka et al., 2019), whether considering full-length transcripts, 5′UTR, 3′UTR, or coding sequence (CDS) portions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by length analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Dendrite-enriched mRNAs show strong enrichment for genes encoding proteins with important roles in the synapse such as synaptic signaling, anterograde synaptic signaling, and behavior.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of dendrite-enriched mRNAs showed strong enrichment for genes encoding proteins with important roles in the synapse such as synaptic signaling, anterograde synaptic signaling, and behavior (Figure 1C), consistent with prior analyses (Cajigas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The GO enrichment for synaptic functions in dendrite-enriched mRNAs is consistent with prior analyses.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of dendrite-enriched mRNAs showed strong enrichment for genes encoding proteins with important roles in the synapse such as synaptic signaling, anterograde synaptic signaling, and behavior (Figure 1C), consistent with prior analyses (Cajigas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with Cajigas et al., 2012.

claim: Kmt2d mRNA is present in dendrites of CA1 neurons.
source: We used RNAscope fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to validate the presence in dendrites of several mRNAs that had not been identified in previous studies including Kmt2d (a histone methyltransferase), Myo5a (an actin motor protein involved in transporting cargo to dendrites), Ppp1r9b (a scaffolding protein component of protein phosphatase 1a important for dendritic spine morphology), and Rbfox2 (a neuronal splicing factor) (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is validated by FISH shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Myo5a mRNA is present in dendrites of CA1 neurons.
source: We used RNAscope fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to validate the presence in dendrites of several mRNAs that had not been identified in previous studies including Kmt2d (a histone methyltransferase), Myo5a (an actin motor protein involved in transporting cargo to dendrites), Ppp1r9b (a scaffolding protein component of protein phosphatase 1a important for dendritic spine morphology), and Rbfox2 (a neuronal splicing factor) (Figure 1D–G).

claim: Different transcripts show variable mRNA distribution patterns in dendrites.
source: Interestingly, approximating the distance from the cell body for each detected mRNA spot revealed variable mRNA distribution patterns for different transcripts, suggesting multiple potential paths for mRNA localization.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH distance analysis.

claim: Variable mRNA distribution patterns suggest multiple potential paths for mRNA localization.
source: Interestingly, approximating the distance from the cell body for each detected mRNA spot revealed variable mRNA distribution patterns for different transcripts, suggesting multiple potential paths for mRNA localization.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed distribution patterns.

claim: Approximately 35% of Kmt2d transcripts were detected throughout the neuropil.
source: For example, roughly 35% of the transcripts encoding Kmt2d and Rbfox2 were detected throughout in the neuropil, whereas ~74% of the transcripts encoding Ppp1r9b were abundant in the distal neuropil (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is quantified from FISH data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Approximately 35% of Rbfox2 transcripts were detected throughout the neuropil.
source: For example, roughly 35% of the transcripts encoding Kmt2d and Rbfox2 were detected throughout in the neuropil, whereas ~74% of the transcripts encoding Ppp1r9b were abundant in the distal neuropil (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is quantified from FISH data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Approximately 74% of Ppp1r9b transcripts were abundant in the distal neuropil.
source: For example, roughly 35% of the transcripts encoding Kmt2d and Rbfox2 were detected throughout in the neuropil, whereas ~74% of the transcripts encoding Ppp1r9b were abundant in the distal neuropil (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is quantified from FISH data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Less than 15% of Snca mRNAs were found in the CA1 neuropil.
source: By comparison, less than 15% of mRNAs encoding alpha-synuclein, a neuronal gene whose protein product is involved in presynaptic transmission (Snca) and an mRNA identified as enriched in the CA1 cell body compartment, were found in the CA1 neuropil.
evidence: This is quantified from FISH data.

claim: Snca encodes alpha-synuclein, a protein involved in presynaptic transmission.
source: By comparison, less than 15% of mRNAs encoding alpha-synuclein, a neuronal gene whose protein product is involved in presynaptic transmission (Snca) and an mRNA identified as enriched in the CA1 cell body compartment, were found in the CA1 neuropil.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Snca function.

claim: Snca mRNA is enriched in the CA1 cell body compartment.
source: By comparison, less than 15% of mRNAs encoding alpha-synuclein, a neuronal gene whose protein product is involved in presynaptic transmission (Snca) and an mRNA identified as enriched in the CA1 cell body compartment, were found in the CA1 neuropil.
evidence: This is identified from the TRAP-seq data.

claim: Subcellular localization of cytoplasmic mRNAs is thought to be at least partially mediated by 3′UTR elements.
source: Subcellular localization of cytoplasmic mRNAs is thought to be at least partially mediated by 3′UTR elements (Andreassi and Riccio, 2009; Blichenberg et al., 2001; Mayford et al., 1996; Tushev et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a model supported by multiple citations.

claim: 15,322 3′UTRs are expressed in Camk2a-expressing pyramidal neurons.
source: This allowed us to identify the boundaries of potential 3′UTRs (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), and revealed 15,322 3′UTRs expressed in Camk2a-expressing pyramidal neurons, including 3700 genes that give rise to mRNAs with more than one 3′UTR isoform.
evidence: This is identified from the combined PAPERCLIP and TRAP analysis.

claim: 3700 genes give rise to mRNAs with more than one 3′UTR isoform in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: This allowed us to identify the boundaries of potential 3′UTRs (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), and revealed 15,322 3′UTRs expressed in Camk2a-expressing pyramidal neurons, including 3700 genes that give rise to mRNAs with more than one 3′UTR isoform.
evidence: This is identified from the combined PAPERCLIP and TRAP analysis.

claim: 219 3′UTR isoforms were differentially localized to CA1 dendrites.
source: Analyzing expression of these 3′UTRs in the compartment-specific TRAP data revealed 219 3′UTR isoforms that were differentially localized to CA1 dendrites (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is identified from DEXSeq analysis of compartment-specific TRAP data.

claim: Of the 219 genes producing differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms, 149 had no effect on the CDS.
source: Of the 219 genes producing differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms in CA1 neurons, we found that 149 had no effect on the CDS, 48 resulted in altered CDS, and 22 generated both event types (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is from analysis of the types of APA events identified.

claim: 48 differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms resulted in altered CDS.
source: Of the 219 genes producing differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms in CA1 neurons, we found that 149 had no effect on the CDS, 48 resulted in altered CDS, and 22 generated both event types (Figure 2B, left panel).

claim: 22 genes generated both 3′UTR-APA and UR-APA events.
source: Of the 219 genes producing differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms in CA1 neurons, we found that 149 had no effect on the CDS, 48 resulted in altered CDS, and 22 generated both event types (Figure 2B, left panel).

claim: Distal 3′UTRs were significantly enriched in dendrites compared to proximal 3′UTRs.

claim: The enrichment of distal 3′UTRs in dendrites is consistent with a previous study by Tushev et al., 2018.
source: Among isoforms with unchanged CDS, distal 3′UTRs were significantly enriched in dendrites, consistent with a previous study of CA1 neuropil RNAs analyzed by 3′ end sequencing (Tushev et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with Tushev et al., 2018.

claim: Proximal 3′UTRs were significantly enriched in the CA1 cell bodies.

evidence: This is from statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Calm1 harbors differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms.
source: We used FISH to validate these types of differential localization events, including Calmodulin 1 (Calm1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E), previously described to harbor differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms (Tushev et al., 2018), F-box protein 31 (Fbxo31) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–H), an E3 ubiquitin ligase proposed to be involved in neuronal maintenance and dendritic outgrowth (Vadhvani et al., 2013), and vesicle-associated membrane protein B (Vapb) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I–K), a membrane protein involved in vesicle trafficking.

claim: Fbxo31 encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase proposed to be involved in neuronal maintenance and dendritic outgrowth.
source: We used FISH to validate these types of differential localization events, including Calmodulin 1 (Calm1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E), previously described to harbor differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms (Tushev et al., 2018), F-box protein 31 (Fbxo31) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–H), an E3 ubiquitin ligase proposed to be involved in neuronal maintenance and dendritic outgrowth (Vadhvani et al., 2013), and vesicle-associated membrane protein B (Vapb) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I–K), a membrane protein involved in vesicle trafficking.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vadhvani et al., 2013.

claim: Vapb encodes a membrane protein involved in vesicle trafficking.
source: We used FISH to validate these types of differential localization events, including Calmodulin 1 (Calm1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E), previously described to harbor differentially localized 3′UTR isoforms (Tushev et al., 2018), F-box protein 31 (Fbxo31) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–H), an E3 ubiquitin ligase proposed to be involved in neuronal maintenance and dendritic outgrowth (Vadhvani et al., 2013), and vesicle-associated membrane protein B (Vapb) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I–K), a membrane protein involved in vesicle trafficking.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Vapb function.

claim: Cnksr2 produces mRNAs with two 3′UTR isoforms: a short isoform highly sequestered in cell bodies and a longer isoform highly localized in the CA1 neuropil.
source: For example, the gene for connector enhancer of kinase suppressor of Ras2 (Cnksr2 or MAGUIN) produces mRNAs with two 3′UTRs isoforms: a short isoform that is highly sequestered in the cell bodies (less than 10% of transcripts were found in the CA1 neuropil by FISH) and a longer isoform of which at least 40% of transcripts were localized in the CA1 neuropil (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is validated by FISH shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: Less than 10% of short Cnksr2 transcripts were found in the CA1 neuropil by FISH.
source: For example, the gene for connector enhancer of kinase suppressor of Ras2 (Cnksr2 or MAGUIN) produces mRNAs with two 3′UTRs isoforms: a short isoform that is highly sequestered in the cell bodies (less than 10% of transcripts were found in the CA1 neuropil by FISH) and a longer isoform of which at least 40% of transcripts were localized in the CA1 neuropil (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is quantified from FISH data in Figure 2C–E.

claim: At least 40% of long Cnksr2 transcripts were localized in the CA1 neuropil.
source: For example, the gene for connector enhancer of kinase suppressor of Ras2 (Cnksr2 or MAGUIN) produces mRNAs with two 3′UTRs isoforms: a short isoform that is highly sequestered in the cell bodies (less than 10% of transcripts were found in the CA1 neuropil by FISH) and a longer isoform of which at least 40% of transcripts were localized in the CA1 neuropil (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is quantified from FISH data in Figure 2C–E.

claim: The protein encoded from the dendritic Cnksr2 mRNA isoform contains an additional PDZ-binding domain not present in the shorter isoform.
source: The protein encoded from the dendritic mRNA isoform contains an additional PDZ-binding domain that is not present in the shorter isoform.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis of the different isoforms.

claim: Cnksr2 has been identified in genome-wide association studies as an ASD candidate.
source: Cnksr2 has been identified in genome-wide association studies as an ASD candidate, and mutations in this gene have been shown to cause epilepsy and intellectual disability (Aypar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aypar et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations in Cnksr2 have been shown to cause epilepsy and intellectual disability.
source: Cnksr2 has been identified in genome-wide association studies as an ASD candidate, and mutations in this gene have been shown to cause epilepsy and intellectual disability (Aypar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aypar et al., 2015.

claim: Anks1b shows differential localization of an isoform generated from 5′ extension of the 3′UTR sequence.
source: Analysis of the ankyrin repeat and sterile alpha motif domain containing 1B (Anks1b) gene revealed differential localization of an isoform generated from 5′ extension of the 3′UTR sequence, which was depleted in the CA1 cell bodies, and again validated by FISH (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is validated by FISH shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: The extended Anks1b isoform was depleted in the CA1 cell bodies.
source: Analysis of the ankyrin repeat and sterile alpha motif domain containing 1B (Anks1b) gene revealed differential localization of an isoform generated from 5′ extension of the 3′UTR sequence, which was depleted in the CA1 cell bodies, and again validated by FISH (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is validated by FISH shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: Ankrd11 produces a full-length version containing Ank repeats and the C-terminal transcriptional repression and activation domain.
source: Finally, two mRNAs produced from the ank-repeat domain containing protein 11 (Ankrd11) gene were identified, a full-length version that contains Ank repeats, as well as the C-terminal transcriptional repression and activation domain, and a previously uncharacterized isoform derived from a polyadenylation site found in intron 8, which is able to produce a protein that contains only the Ank-repeat regions (see PAPERCLIP profile in Figure 2I).
evidence: This is identified from PAPERCLIP and sequence analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Ankrd11 produces a previously uncharacterized isoform derived from a polyadenylation site in intron 8 that contains only the Ank-repeat regions.
source: Finally, two mRNAs produced from the ank-repeat domain containing protein 11 (Ankrd11) gene were identified, a full-length version that contains Ank repeats, as well as the C-terminal transcriptional repression and activation domain, and a previously uncharacterized isoform derived from a polyadenylation site found in intron 8, which is able to produce a protein that contains only the Ank-repeat regions (see PAPERCLIP profile in Figure 2I).
evidence: This is identified from PAPERCLIP analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The truncated Ankrd11 isoform was predominantly detected in the cell bodies of CA1 neurons by both TRAP and FISH.
source: The truncated isoform was predominantly detected in the cell bodies of CA1 neurons by both TRAP and FISH, while the full-length isoform was detected in both the cell bodies and dendrites (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is shown by TRAP and FISH data in Figure 2I–K.

claim: The full-length Ankrd11 isoform was detected in both cell bodies and dendrites.
source: The truncated isoform was predominantly detected in the cell bodies of CA1 neurons by both TRAP and FISH, while the full-length isoform was detected in both the cell bodies and dendrites (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is shown by TRAP and FISH data in Figure 2I–K.

claim: Dendritic transcripts with altered protein-coding capacity are generated by alternative processing of 3′UTRs.
source: Together, these data demonstrate the utility of combining compartment- and cell-type transcriptomics and PAPERCLIP to define expressed 3′UTRs and reveal that dendritic transcripts with altered protein-coding capacity are generated by alternative processing of 3′UTRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on APA events.

claim: 165 AS events in 143 genes were differentially expressed between CA1 cell bodies and dendrites.
source: After analysis with rMATS (Shen et al., 2014) and filtering, we identified 165 AS events in 143 genes that were differentially expressed between the two compartments (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This is identified from rMATS analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Of the 165 differentially localized AS events, 106 (64.2%) were skipped exons.
source: Of these, 106 (64.2%) were skipped exons, 32 (19.4%) were alternative 3′ splice sites, 14 (8.5%) were alternative 5′ splice sites, and 13 (7.9%) were mutually exclusive exons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from classification of AS events shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 32 (19.4%) of the differentially localized AS events were alternative 3′ splice sites.
source: Of these, 106 (64.2%) were skipped exons, 32 (19.4%) were alternative 3′ splice sites, 14 (8.5%) were alternative 5′ splice sites, and 13 (7.9%) were mutually exclusive exons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from classification of AS events shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 14 (8.5%) of the differentially localized AS events were alternative 5′ splice sites.
source: Of these, 106 (64.2%) were skipped exons, 32 (19.4%) were alternative 3′ splice sites, 14 (8.5%) were alternative 5′ splice sites, and 13 (7.9%) were mutually exclusive exons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from classification of AS events shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 13 (7.9%) of the differentially localized AS events were mutually exclusive exons.
source: Of these, 106 (64.2%) were skipped exons, 32 (19.4%) were alternative 3′ splice sites, 14 (8.5%) were alternative 5′ splice sites, and 13 (7.9%) were mutually exclusive exons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from classification of AS events shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Alternatively spliced transcripts encode proteins involved in synaptic functions such as action potential, receptor localization, and synaptic signaling, as well as mRNA splicing.
source: These alternatively spliced transcripts encode proteins involved in synaptic functions such as action potential, receptor localization, and synaptic signaling, as well as mRNA splicing (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is from GO analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MBNL1/2 regulates 37 differentially localized AS events.
source: Of these, MBNL1/2 (using data from Weyn-Vanhentenryck et al., 2018) and NOVA2 (using data from Saito et al., 2016) were found to regulate the largest number of these events (37 for MBNL1/2 and 36 for NOVA2, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is from analysis comparing differentially localized AS events with RNA-binding protein KO data, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NOVA2 regulates 36 differentially localized AS events.
source: Of these, MBNL1/2 (using data from Weyn-Vanhentenryck et al., 2018) and NOVA2 (using data from Saito et al., 2016) were found to regulate the largest number of these events (37 for MBNL1/2 and 36 for NOVA2, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is from analysis comparing differentially localized AS events with RNA-binding protein KO data, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CA1 neuropil/cell body splicing changes were positively correlated with splicing changes in NOVA2 KO animals (Pearson coefficient = 0.498, p-value=9.87e-08).
source: Interestingly, we found that CA1 neuropil/cell body splicing changes were positively correlated with splicing changes in NOVA2 KO animals (from analysis of Nova2-null vs. WT data, Pearson coefficient = 0.498, p-value=9.87e-08), which indicates that NOVA2 drives splicing changes that result in mRNAs that are preferentially sequestered in CA1 cell bodies (Figure 3E, left panel).
evidence: This is from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: NOVA2 drives splicing changes that result in mRNAs preferentially sequestered in CA1 cell bodies.
source: Interestingly, we found that CA1 neuropil/cell body splicing changes were positively correlated with splicing changes in NOVA2 KO animals (from analysis of Nova2-null vs. WT data, Pearson coefficient = 0.498, p-value=9.87e-08), which indicates that NOVA2 drives splicing changes that result in mRNAs that are preferentially sequestered in CA1 cell bodies (Figure 3E, left panel).
evidence: This is inferred from the positive correlation between NOVA2-dependent splicing and cell body enrichment.

claim: MBNL1/2-dependent splicing changes did not show correlation with localized splicing changes (Pearson coefficient = –0.00438, p-value=0.9698).
source: This effect was specific for NOVA2 as MBNL1/2-dependent splicing changes did not show such a correlation with the localized splicing changes (Pearson coefficient = –0.00438, p-value=0.9698, Figure 3E, right panel).
evidence: This is from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Rapgef4 (Epac2) encodes a cAMP-activated guanine exchange factor for RAP1 and RAP2 involved in LTP in the hippocampus.
source: Rapgef4 (Epac2), the gene encoding a cAMP-activated guanine exchange factor for RAP1 and RAP2 involved in LTP in the hippocampus, expresses two isoforms in the brain, a full-length isoform (Epac2A1), and one that is lacking exon 7 (Epac2A2) (Hoivik et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hoivik et al., 2013.

claim: Rapgef4 expresses two isoforms in the brain: Epac2A1 (full-length) and Epac2A2 (lacking exon 7).
source: Rapgef4 (Epac2), the gene encoding a cAMP-activated guanine exchange factor for RAP1 and RAP2 involved in LTP in the hippocampus, expresses two isoforms in the brain, a full-length isoform (Epac2A1), and one that is lacking exon 7 (Epac2A2) (Hoivik et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoivik et al., 2013.

claim: Only 25% of Rapgef4 transcripts detected in CA1 dendrites included exon 7, whereas in cell bodies 75% contained exon 7.
source: Of the Rapgef4 transcripts detected in the CA1 dendrites, only 25% included exon 7, whereas in the cell bodies, 75% of the Rapgef4 contained exon 7 (Figure 3F), indicating preferential localization of the transcripts without exon 7 to the CA1 dendrites.
evidence: This is quantified from TRAP data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Rapgef4 transcripts without exon 7 are preferentially localized to CA1 dendrites.
source: Of the Rapgef4 transcripts detected in the CA1 dendrites, only 25% included exon 7, whereas in the cell bodies, 75% of the Rapgef4 contained exon 7 (Figure 3F), indicating preferential localization of the transcripts without exon 7 to the CA1 dendrites.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential exon inclusion patterns in different compartments.

claim: Nnat is a maternally imprinted gene whose protein is important for regulation of intracellular calcium levels.
source: Nnat, a maternally imprinted gene whose protein is important for regulation of intracellular calcium levels, is expressed as either an α- and β-isoform in which exon 2 is included or skipped, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nnat.

claim: Nnat is expressed as α- and β-isoforms in which exon 2 is included or skipped, respectively.
source: Nnat, a maternally imprinted gene whose protein is important for regulation of intracellular calcium levels, is expressed as either an α- and β-isoform in which exon 2 is included or skipped, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nnat isoforms.

claim: Nnat transcripts lacking exon 2 are predominantly sequestered in cell bodies, with only ~12.5% of cell body transcripts containing exon 2.
source: We found that Nnat transcripts lacking exon 2 are predominantly sequestered in the cell bodies, with only ~12.5% of cell body transcripts containing exon 2.
evidence: This is quantified from TRAP data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The majority of localized Nnat transcripts (50–75%) contain exon 2.
source: Conversely, the majority of localized Nnat transcripts (50–75%) contain exon 2, indicating preferential localization of the exon 2 containing Nnat transcripts (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is quantified from TRAP data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Nnat transcripts containing exon 2 are preferentially localized to dendrites.
source: Conversely, the majority of localized Nnat transcripts (50–75%) contain exon 2, indicating preferential localization of the exon 2 containing Nnat transcripts (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential exon inclusion patterns.

claim: Dendritic transcripts with altered protein-coding capacity are generated by both APA and AS.
source: These observations underscore the role of AS in generation of localized transcript isoforms. More generally, these data demonstrate that dendritic transcripts with altered protein-coding capacity are generated by both APA and AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined APA and AS analyses.

claim: CA1 FMRP targets are significantly overrepresented in dendrite-present mRNAs.
source: We observed significant overrepresentation of FMRP targets in dendrite-present mRNAs, and even more so in dendrite-enriched mRNAs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CA1 FMRP targets are even more overrepresented in dendrite-enriched mRNAs than in dendrite-present mRNAs.
source: We observed significant overrepresentation of FMRP targets in dendrite-present mRNAs, and even more so in dendrite-enriched mRNAs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: About 35% (413 mRNAs) of 1211 dendrite-enriched mRNAs were FMRP targets.
source: Of 1211 dendrite-enriched mRNAs, about 35% (413 mRNAs) were FMRP targets compared to 28.5% of dendrite-present mRNAs and 11.6% of all CA1-expressed mRNAs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 28.5% of dendrite-present mRNAs were FMRP targets.
source: Of 1211 dendrite-enriched mRNAs, about 35% (413 mRNAs) were FMRP targets compared to 28.5% of dendrite-present mRNAs and 11.6% of all CA1-expressed mRNAs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 11.6% of all CA1-expressed mRNAs were FMRP targets.
source: Of 1211 dendrite-enriched mRNAs, about 35% (413 mRNAs) were FMRP targets compared to 28.5% of dendrite-present mRNAs and 11.6% of all CA1-expressed mRNAs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dendrite-enriched mRNAs that are CA1 FMRP targets are significantly more abundant in dendrites than dendritic non-FMRP targets.
source: Dendrite-enriched mRNAs that are also CA1 FMRP targets are significantly more abundant in dendrites than dendritic non-FMRP targets. Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to determine significance (****p<0.00001).
evidence: This is from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FMRP-bound dendritic mRNAs are significantly longer than nontargets.
source: Further characterization of these dendrite-enriched mRNAs revealed that they were generally longer than all CA1-expressed mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but that FMRP-bound dendritic mRNAs were significantly longer than the nontargets (p-value=9.13e-46, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is from length analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FMRP preferentially binds long mRNAs.
source: These observations were consistent with prior observations that FMRP preferentially binds long mRNAs (Darnell et al., 2011; Sawicka et al., 2019), and taken together, suggest that FMRP binds the majority of long, dendritic mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FMRP binds the majority of long, dendritic mRNAs.
source: These observations were consistent with prior observations that FMRP preferentially binds long mRNAs (Darnell et al., 2011; Sawicka et al., 2019), and taken together, suggest that FMRP binds the majority of long, dendritic mRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FMRP-bound dendritic mRNAs are longer.

claim: Dendrite-enriched FMRP targets are enriched for proteins involved in synaptic signaling, behavior, regulation of trans-synaptic signaling, and GTPase-mediated signal transduction.
source: Examination of the functional differences between dendrite-enriched FMRP targets and nontargets revealed an enrichment in dendritic FMRP targets for proteins involved in synaptic signaling, behavior, regulation of trans-synaptic signaling, and GTPase-mediated signal transduction (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is from GO analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: FMRP is a key regulator of local translation in the dendrite of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in important synaptic functions.
source: These data indicate that FMRP is a key regulator of local translation in the dendrite of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in important synaptic functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional enrichment of dendritic FMRP targets.

claim: All dendrite-enriched mRNAs are highly G- and C-rich.
source: Importantly, we found that all dendrite-enriched mRNAs are highly G- and C-rich (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D), so we analyzed differences in G-quadruplex containing transcripts between dendrite-enriched FMRP targets and dendrite-enriched non-FMRP targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is from sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: There is no evidence for significant enrichment of experimentally defined G-quadruplexes in dendrite-enriched FMRP targets compared to non-FMRP targets.
source: We searched for experimentally defined G-quadruplexes (Guo and Bartel, 2016; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and also predicted G-quadruplex motifs (as defined in Goering et al., 2020) in the 3′UTRs of dendrite-enriched FMRP targets and FMRP nontargets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F). We found no evidence for significant enrichment of G-quadruplexes in dendrite-enriched FMRP targets.
evidence: This is from analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There is no evidence for significant enrichment of predicted G-quadruplex motifs in dendrite-enriched FMRP targets compared to non-FMRP targets.
source: We searched for experimentally defined G-quadruplexes (Guo and Bartel, 2016; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and also predicted G-quadruplex motifs (as defined in Goering et al., 2020) in the 3′UTRs of dendrite-enriched FMRP targets and FMRP nontargets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F). We found no evidence for significant enrichment of G-quadruplexes in dendrite-enriched FMRP targets.
evidence: This is from analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Dendrite-enriched mRNAs have significantly higher FMRP CLIP scores than dendrite-present mRNAs.
source: Dendrite-enriched mRNAs had significantly higher FMRP CLIP scores and hence greater FMRP binding than the dendrite-present group (p-value=2.646e-05, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: FMRP CLIP scores positively correlate with relative abundance in dendrites.
source: Additionally, FMRP CLIP scores positively correlated with relative abundance in dendrites: when CA1 mRNAs were grouped according to the magnitude of their CA1 FMRP CLIP scores, those with increasingly higher scores were increasingly abundant in dendrites (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: FMRP binds mRNAs that are more abundant in dendrites than in cell bodies.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that FMRP binds mRNAs that are more abundant in dendrites than in cell bodies.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between FMRP binding and dendritic abundance.

claim: The magnitude of CA1 FMRP CLIP scores is predictive of the relative dendritic abundance of FMRP targets.
source: Moreover, the magnitude of CA1 FMRP CLIP scores are predictive of the relative dendritic abundance of its targets (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CA1 FMRP-CLIP tags were detected on the long, dendritic isoform of Ankrd11, but only sparsely on the short isoform.
source: For example, the Ankrd11 transcript undergoes APA to express a short and long isoform, and only the long isoform is abundant on dendritic ribosomes (Figure 2I–K). Interestingly, CA1 FMRP-CLIP tags were detected on the long, dendritic isoform, but only sparsely on the short isoform (Figure 5A, gray dashed boxes).
evidence: This is shown in the CLIP data in Figure 5A.

claim: FMRP binding was largely absent on the shorter, cell body-enriched isoform of Cnksr2, while robust binding was evident on the longer, dendritic 3′UTR.
source: For example, FMRP binding was largely absent on a shorter, CB-enriched isoform of the Cnksr2 transcript, while robust binding was evident on the longer, dendritic 3′UTR (Figure 5B, gray dashed boxes).
evidence: This is shown in the CLIP data in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 80% of FMRP-bound Cnksr2 transcripts derived from the longer, dendritic isoform.
source: Of the 12 exon junction reads that originated from exon 20 of the Cnksr2 transcript, 10 were derived from the long isoform, suggesting that approximately 80% of the FMRP-bound Cnksr2 transcripts derived from the longer, dendritic isoform.
evidence: This is calculated from junction reads in FMRP-CLIP data.

claim: The shorter Cnksr2 isoform was the predominant isoform in CA1 pyramidal neurons (~80% of exon junction reads in cell body TRAP).
source: This was especially striking since the shorter isoform was the predominant isoform in CA1 pyramidal neurons (~80% of exon junction reads in cell body TRAP belonged to the short isoform), indicating a high degree of selectivity of FMRP binding to this dendritic isoform (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is from TRAP junction read analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FMRP shows a high degree of selectivity in binding to the dendritic Cnksr2 isoform.
source: This was especially striking since the shorter isoform was the predominant isoform in CA1 pyramidal neurons (~80% of exon junction reads in cell body TRAP belonged to the short isoform), indicating a high degree of selectivity of FMRP binding to this dendritic isoform (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the preferential FMRP binding to the less abundant dendritic isoform.

claim: Splicing events identified in FMRP-bound mRNAs show stronger correlation with PSI values in CA1 neuropil TRAP relative to cell body TRAP.
source: Globally, we compared the percent spliced in (PSI) values for the 17 detected alternative splice events detected in FMRP-CLIP with those in the CA1 cell body and neuropil TRAP data. This revealed that splicing events identified in FMRP-bound mRNAs show stronger correlation with PSI values determined in CA1 neuropil TRAP relative to cell body TRAP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FMRP preferentially binds to specific processed transcripts that are fated for dendritic localization.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that FMRP preferentially binds to specific processed transcripts that are fated for dendritic localization.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective binding patterns and correlation with dendritic isoforms.

claim: 746,827 FMRP CA1-specific CLIP tags were obtained from cell bodies across five biological replicates.
source: Across five biological replicates, we obtained 746,827 FMRP CA1-specific CLIP tags from the cell bodies and 80,749 tags from CA1 dendrites.
evidence: This is a direct count from the CLIP experiments.

claim: 80,749 FMRP CA1-specific CLIP tags were obtained from CA1 dendrites across five biological replicates.
source: Across five biological replicates, we obtained 746,827 FMRP CA1-specific CLIP tags from the cell bodies and 80,749 tags from CA1 dendrites.
evidence: This is a direct count from the CLIP experiments.

claim: A similar distribution of FMRP CLIP tags was observed across the CDS in mRNAs from cell bodies and dendrites.
source: Overall, we observed a similar distribution of FMRP CLIP tags across the CDS in these mRNAs and in the two compartments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with prior CLIP analysis and the general observation that FMRP binds CDS to arrest ribosomal elongation (Darnell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution of FMRP CLIP tags is consistent with prior CLIP analysis and the observation that FMRP binds CDS to arrest ribosomal elongation.
source: Overall, we observed a similar distribution of FMRP CLIP tags across the CDS in these mRNAs and in the two compartments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with prior CLIP analysis and the general observation that FMRP binds CDS to arrest ribosomal elongation (Darnell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darnell et al., 2011.

claim: 383 dendritic FMRP targets were identified, defined as mRNAs reproducibly bound by FMRP in CA1 dendrites.
source: From this, we identified 383 'dendritic FMRP targets,' defined as mRNAs that are reproducibly bound by FMRP in CA1 dendrites (Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: This is from the compartment-specific FMRP-CLIP analysis.

claim: 60.8% (233) of dendritic FMRP targets were dendrite-enriched mRNAs.
source: Of these dendritic FMRP targets, 60.8% (233) were mRNAs defined in Figure 1 as dendrite-enriched (Figure 6B) and 76.5% (293) were dendrite-present (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is from overlap analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 76.5% (293) of dendritic FMRP targets were dendrite-present mRNAs.
source: Of these dendritic FMRP targets, 60.8% (233) were mRNAs defined in Figure 1 as dendrite-enriched (Figure 6B) and 76.5% (293) were dendrite-present (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is from overlap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dendritic FMRP targets show greater relative abundance in ribosome-bound mRNAs (TRAP) when compared to all CA1 FMRP targets.
source: Dendritic FMRP targets show greater relative abundance in ribosome-bound mRNAs (TRAP) when compared to all CA1 FMRP targets (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is from analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: FMRP-CLIP scores for dendritic FMRP targets were significantly larger than scores for the full set of dendrite-enriched mRNAs.
source: Additionally, when comparing the FMRP-CLIP scores identified previously by whole hippocampus CA1 FMRP-CLIP, the FMRP-CLIP scores for the dendritic FMRP targets were significantly larger than the scores for the full set of dendrite-enriched mRNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is from statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Dendritic FMRP targets are a subset of previously identified FMRP targets.
source: These data suggest that dendritic FMRP targets are a subset of previously identified FMRP targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher CLIP scores and overlap with previous targets.

claim: Some experimentally defined dendritic FMRP targets had low levels of whole-cell FMRP binding (negative CA1 FMRP CLIP scores).
source: Interestingly, we identified a number of experimentally defined dendritic FMRP targets that had low levels of whole-cell FMRP cell binding (i.e., had negative CA1 FMRP CLIP scores, Figure 6D), indicating that these mRNAs are significantly more FMRP-bound in dendrites than in cell bodies.
evidence: This is from analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Some mRNAs are significantly more FMRP-bound in dendrites than in cell bodies.
source: Interestingly, we identified a number of experimentally defined dendritic FMRP targets that had low levels of whole-cell FMRP cell binding (i.e., had negative CA1 FMRP CLIP scores, Figure 6D), indicating that these mRNAs are significantly more FMRP-bound in dendrites than in cell bodies.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative whole-cell CLIP scores but positive dendritic CLIP scores.

claim: Three functional modules (FM1, FM2, FM3) were detected among CA1 FMRP targets, with more than 100 genes each.
source: To test this, we segregated all whole-cell CA1 FMRP CLIP targets according to their function by module detection using the HumanBase software (Krishnan et al., 2016). Eight functional modules were detected, three of which contained more than 100 genes (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: This is from functional module detection shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The FM1 cluster contains 393 genes highly enriched for genes involved in nuclear regulation of gene expression.
source: The FM1 cluster, which contains 393 genes, is highly enriched for genes involved in nuclear regulation of gene expression, with the top GO terms being chromatin organization and modification and histone modification.
evidence: This is from GO analysis of the FM1 cluster.

claim: The top GO terms for FM1 are chromatin organization and modification and histone modification.
source: The FM1 cluster, which contains 393 genes, is highly enriched for genes involved in nuclear regulation of gene expression, with the top GO terms being chromatin organization and modification and histone modification.
evidence: This is from GO analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: FM2 contains 292 genes enriched for genes involved in ion transport and receptor signaling.
source: FM2 (292 genes) is enriched for genes involved in ion transport and receptor signaling.
evidence: This is from GO analysis of the FM2 cluster.

claim: The FM3 cluster contains 203 genes involved in maintenance of cell polarity and autophagy.
source: The FM3 cluster (203 genes) contains genes involved in the maintenance of cell polarity and autophagy (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is from GO analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: FM2 and FM3 clusters were highly enriched in FMRP-bound mRNAs in both dendrites and cell bodies.
source: FM2 and FM3 clusters were highly enriched in FMRP-bound mRNAs in both the dendrites and the cell bodies, while the FM1 cluster was strongly enriched among cell body-bound FMRP targets, but only weakly enriched among the dendritic FMRP-bound transcripts (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is from GSEA shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The FM1 cluster was strongly enriched among cell body-bound FMRP targets, but only weakly enriched among dendritic FMRP-bound transcripts.
source: FM2 and FM3 clusters were highly enriched in FMRP-bound mRNAs in both the dendrites and the cell bodies, while the FM1 cluster was strongly enriched among cell body-bound FMRP targets, but only weakly enriched among the dendritic FMRP-bound transcripts (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is from GSEA shown in Figure 7C.

claim: FM2 and FM3 modules contain mRNAs that are directly bound and regulated by FMRP in dendrites.
source: This suggests that FM2 and FM3 modules contain mRNAs that are directly bound and regulated by FMRP in dendrites, and the FM1 cluster contains highly bound FMRP targets in the cell bodies, indicating distinct, biologically coherent regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential enrichment patterns in GSEA.

claim: The FM1 cluster contains highly bound FMRP targets in cell bodies.
source: This suggests that FM2 and FM3 modules contain mRNAs that are directly bound and regulated by FMRP in dendrites, and the FM1 cluster contains highly bound FMRP targets in the cell bodies, indicating distinct, biologically coherent regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential enrichment patterns in GSEA.

claim: FMRP shows distinct, biologically coherent regulation of different functional modules in different compartments.
source: This suggests that FM2 and FM3 modules contain mRNAs that are directly bound and regulated by FMRP in dendrites, and the FM1 cluster contains highly bound FMRP targets in the cell bodies, indicating distinct, biologically coherent regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the compartment-specific enrichment of functional modules.

claim: The AM2 module contains transcripts enriched for glutamate signaling, learning, and memory, and is bound by FMRP in both dendrites and cell bodies.
source: One module, AM2, contains transcripts enriched for glutamate signaling, learning, and memory, and is bound by FMRP in both the dendrites and cell bodies.
evidence: This is from functional module analysis of ASD candidate genes shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The AM1 module consists of genes involved in chromatin modification and is highly enriched among mRNAs bound by FMRP in cell bodies, but not significantly enriched among dendritic FMRP-bound mRNAs.
source: The AM1 module consists of genes involved in chromatin modification and is highly enriched among mRNAs bound by FMRP in the cell bodies, but is not significantly enriched among dendritic FMRP-bound mRNAs.
evidence: This is from GSEA of ASD candidate gene modules shown in Figure 7D.

claim: FMRP may have compartmentalized roles, regulating mRNAs important for synaptic signaling near synapses and mRNAs involved in chromatin regulation in cell bodies.
source: Taken together these observations suggest the possibility of compartmentalized roles for FMRP, in which mRNAs important for synaptic signaling are bound and regulated by FMRP near the synapses, while mRNAs bound by FMRP in the cell bodies are involved in the regulation of neuronal gene expression through chromatin regulation.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the compartment-specific functional enrichment patterns.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq of microdissected material in FMRP WT and KO mice showed no overall change in the localization of FMRP targets.
source: Bulk RNA-seq of microdissected material in FMRP WT and KO mice showed no overall change in the localization of FMRP targets (Figure 7E, left panel).
evidence: This is from bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: mRNAs found to be dendrite-present and dendrite-enriched in KO animals show large overlap with those in WT animals.
source: In addition, the mRNAs found to be dendrite-present and dendrite-enriched in KO animals (as in Figure 1, Supplementary file 1K) show large overlap with those in WT animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is from overlap analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: FISH in FMRP KO mouse brain slices found no evidence for altered localization of FMRP targets into the neuropil.
source: We validated this finding by FISH in FMRP KO mouse brain slices and found no evidence for altered localization of FMRP targets into the neuropil (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is validated by FISH shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Global analysis of 3′UTR usage differences in TRAP between dendrites and cell bodies in FMRP KO and WT animals showed no significant instances of dysregulated localization of 3′UTR isoforms in FMRP KO animals.
source: Global analysis of 3′UTR usage differences in TRAP between dendrites and cell bodies in FMRP KO and WT animals also showed no significant (FDR < 0.05) instances of dysregulated localization of 3′UTR isoforms in FMRP KO animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is from DEXSeq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: FISH in FMRP KO mice revealed no differences in isoform localization for Cnksr2 or Anks1b mRNAs.
source: We validated this finding using FISH in FMRP KO mice, which revealed no differences in isoform localization for Cnksr2 or Anks1b mRNAs (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is validated by FISH shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Dendritic mRNA levels of ribosome-associated FMRP targets were increased in CA1 dendrites of KO mice.
source: Although the identities of the dendritic mRNAs found in FMRP WT and KO mice were similar, quantitative analysis of TRAP revealed that dendritic mRNA levels of ribosome-associated FMRP targets were increased in CA1 dendrites of KO mice (Figure 7E, right panel).
evidence: This is from TRAP analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The increase in ribosome-associated FMRP targets in dendrites was evident for FM2/3, but not FM1 transcripts.
source: Interestingly, this was evident for FM2/3, but not FM1 transcripts.
evidence: This is from analysis of functional modules in TRAP data.

claim: FMRP targets are generally downregulated in TRAP from hippocampal neurons.
source: While FMRP targets are generally downregulated in TRAP from hippocampal neurons (Sawicka et al., 2019), a finding that we replicate in cell bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A), transcripts that encode synaptic regulatory proteins (FM2/3), which are bound by FMRP in the dendrites, show increased ribosome association in CA1 dendrites of KO animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawicka et al., 2019 and replicated in the current study.

claim: Transcripts encoding synaptic regulatory proteins (FM2/3) show increased ribosome association in CA1 dendrites of KO animals.
source: While FMRP targets are generally downregulated in TRAP from hippocampal neurons (Sawicka et al., 2019), a finding that we replicate in cell bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A), transcripts that encode synaptic regulatory proteins (FM2/3), which are bound by FMRP in the dendrites, show increased ribosome association in CA1 dendrites of KO animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is from TRAP analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In the absence of FMRP, transcripts that are normally FMRP targets can still be localized to dendrites, but have increased ribosome association.
source: This suggests that in the absence of FMRP, while transcripts that are normally FMRP targets can still be localized to dendrites, they have an increased ribosome association.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that localization is unchanged but ribosome association is increased in FMRP KO.

claim: The findings support the proposal that FMRP in neuronal processes may exist in a polyribosome-depleted granule, which becomes translationally competent upon neuronal activity.
source: This supports the proposal (Wang et al., 2008) that FMRP in the neuronal processes may exist in a polyribosome-depleted granule, which is altered to become translationally competent upon neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2008 and the current data.

claim: The findings are consistent with the role of FMRP as a translational suppressor.
source: It is also consistent with the role of FMRP as a translational suppressor and detection of increased basal translation rates in mouse models of Fragile X syndrome (Gross et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing increased translation in FMRP KO models.

claim: Increased basal translation rates have been detected in mouse models of Fragile X syndrome.
source: It is also consistent with the role of FMRP as a translational suppressor and detection of increased basal translation rates in mouse models of Fragile X syndrome (Gross et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gross et al., 2010 and Liu et al., 2012.
